Fig. 4(a) and (b) reveals that the microstructure of an unstressed, isothermally oxidized 75 alloy specimen goes from a moderately coarse, grainy structure at 700 ◦C to a coarser, more heavily faceted structure at 800 ◦C.
Fig. 4(c) illustrates that applied stress causes the degree of faceting to be reduced, and a finer, more nodular structure develops.

Fig. 5(a) and (b) reveals that the microstructure of an unstressed, isothermally oxidized 230 alloy specimen goes from a fine, highly faceted microstructure at 700 ◦C to a much coarser faceted microstructure at 800 ◦C.
Applied stress causes the microstructure of the 230 alloy [Fig. 5(c)] to be finer and more nodular.
It is believed that the applied stress caused more defects to form in the grain boundaries of the alloys.
Applied stresses may influence diffusivities in a material by increasing dislocation densities [19,20].
These grain and grain boundary defects acted as fast diffusion paths for Cr atoms, increased the flux of Cr (JCr) in the stressed specimens, and resulted in a faster formation of Cr2O3.

The faster formation of protective Cr2O3 reduced the transient oxidation period, improved oxidation resistance in the stressed specimens over the intermediate time period, and resulted in the thinner oxides and lower specific mass change values.
This deformation is attributed to simultaneous cracking and rapid healing of the oxide layer known as pseudoplasticity [19,20,28,29].
The 230 alloy specimens demonstrated better creep resistance than the 75 alloy specimens, likely due to compositional differences and larger average grain size.
